Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 43, verse 1–10:

(p-301) Surat az-Zukhruf

It is a Meccan surah by the consensus (ijma') of the scholars.

Muqatil said: It is Meccan, except for one verse, which is His saying: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you as messengers﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 45].

(p-302) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ha-Mim﴾. Its explanation has already passed (in the commentary on Surat al-Mu'min).

﴿By the Clear Book﴾: an oath by the Qur'an.

﴿Indeed, We have made it﴾: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "We have sent it down." The rest of this has already been explained (in the commentary on Surat an-Nisa' [82] and Surat Yusuf [2]), up to His saying: ﴿And indeed it﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿is in the Mother of the Book﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, in the origin of the Book. The origin of everything is its mother, and the Qur'an is recorded with Allah, mighty and majestic, in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In Our presence﴾, that is, with Us, ﴿exalted﴾, that is, lofty.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿Wise﴾ there are two views. The first: "firmly established" (muhkam), that is, protected from falsehood; this was said by Muqatil. The second: "judging" for the people of faith with Paradise and for the people of disbelief with the Fire; this was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The meaning is: if you deny it, O people of Makkah, then it is with Us honored and of great standing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall We then turn away the reminder from you, altogether, because you are a transgressing people?﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, We withhold from you and do not mention you, "safhan," meaning turning away. It is said: "I turned away (safahtu) from so-and-so" when I turned away from him. The origin of this is that you turn to him the side (safhah) of your neck. Kuthayyir said describing a woman:

"Averse, so you do not meet her except as a stingy one; whoever tires of that union, she tires of it."

That is, turning away with her face. It is said: "I struck (darabtu) from so-and-so such-and-such" when you withhold it and turn away from it. ﴿An kuntum﴾: Ibn Kathir, Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "an kuntum" with a fatha, meaning "because you are a people who are transgressing." Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "in kuntum" with a kasra on the hamzah. Al-Zajjaj said: this is in the sense of the future, that is, if you are transgressing, We will turn away the reminder from you.

Regarding what is meant by "the reminder" there are two views.

The first: it is the mention of the punishment. The meaning is: "Shall We withhold Our punishment from you and leave you in your disbelief?!" This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: it is the Qur'an. The meaning is: "Shall We withhold the sending down of the Qur'an because you do not believe in it?!" This is the meaning of the statement of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

Qatadah said: "musrifin" means "mushrikin" (polytheists).

Then He informed His Prophet that I have sent messengers before, and they were denied, so I destroyed those who denied, by the signs which follow these.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Stronger than them﴾, that is, than the Quraysh, ﴿in might﴾, that is, in strength. ﴿And the example of the former peoples has passed﴾, that is, the description of their punishment has already preceded in what was revealed to you. It was also said: the comparison of their state with these in denial has preceded, so resemblance between them in destruction will occur.

Then He informed of their ignorance when they acknowledged that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and then worshipped other than Him, by the verse which follows this; then the one that follows it is explained in [Ta-Ha: 53], up to His saying: ﴿so that you may be guided﴾, that is, so that you may be guided in your journeys to your destinations.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn ʿAmir recited "tukhrajūn" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the ra'; the rest recited it with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the ra'. What follows this has already been discussed [Ya-Sin: 36, 42] up to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that you may sit firmly upon its back﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: the pronoun of the masculine (hā' al-tadhkīr) refers to "mā" (that which).

﴿Then you may remember the favor of your Lord﴾ when He subjected that vehicle to you on land and sea. ﴿And we were not able to control it﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: meaning, "capable of it" (mutīqīn). Ibn Qutayba said: it is said, "anā muqrinun laka," meaning, "I am capable of you." It is also said that it comes from their saying, "anā qirnun li-fulān" when you are his equal in strength. If you say, "anā qarnun li-fulān" with a fatha on the qaf, its meaning is that you are his equal in age. Abu ʿUbayda said: "muqrinīn" means "controlling" (ḍābiṭīn); it is said, "fulān muqrinun li-fulān," meaning he controls him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, to our Lord we will surely return﴾, meaning: returning in the Hereafter.

Al-Musayyabi related from Nafi': "aʾ-shhidū" (ʾ-shhidū), elongated, from ashhadtu (I made them witness), while the rest do not elongate.

"Ashhidū" (a-shhidū) is from shahidtu (I witnessed), meaning: did they attend it, so that they knew that they are females?! This is a rebuke to them, since they spoke about something known only through witnessing without having witnessed it. ﴿Their testimony will be recorded﴾ regarding the angels, that they are daughters of Allah. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 43, verses 26–30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I am free (barra') [of what you worship]﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-bara'" means "al-bari'" (free from). The Arabs say to one person, "I am al-bara' from you," and the same form is used for two people, for a group, for the masculine and for the feminine. They say, "We are al-bara' from you and al-khala' from you," and they do not say, "We are al-barra'an from you" or "al-barra'un from you." The meaning is: "I am one who is free (dhu al-bara') from you, and we are those who are free (dhawu al-bara') from you," just as one says, "a man who is just (adl)" and "a woman who is just (adl)." We have already explained Abraham's exception of his Lord, mighty and majestic, from what they worship, at His saying: ﴿except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He made it﴾, meaning the word of tawhid (the declaration of God's oneness), which is "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah), ﴿a word that remains in his posterity﴾, meaning among those who come after him from his offspring, so that there will always be a monotheist among them, ﴿so that they may return﴾ to tawhid, all of them, when they hear that their father disassociated himself from the idols and affirmed the oneness of Allah, mighty and majestic.

Then He mentioned His favour upon the Quraysh, saying: ﴿Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and to their fathers﴾. The meaning is: I bestowed abundant blessings upon them and did not hasten to punish them, ﴿until there came to them the truth﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿and a clear messenger﴾, who is Muhammad (ﷺ). It was therefore fitting for them to repay the blessings with obedience to the Messenger, but they opposed him.

﴿And when the truth came to them﴾: this refers to the Quraysh according to the saying of most scholars. Qatadah said: they are the Jews. "Al-Haqq" is the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 43, verse 31–35:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of great standing from the two cities?"﴾ That is, "Why not?" ﴿sent down upon a man of great standing from the two cities.﴾ As for the two cities, they are Makkah and al-Ta'if; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority. As for the great man of Makkah, there are two opinions.

One of them: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Qurashi. Al-'Awfi and others related it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah and al-Suddi also said so.

The second: 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah. This was said by Mujahid.

As for the great man of al-Ta'if, there are five opinions.

The first: Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi. Al-'Awfi related it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Mas'ud ibn 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd Allah. Al-Dahhak related it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that he is Abu Mas'ud 'Urwah ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Layth related it from Mujahid, and Qatadah also said so.

The fourth: [that he is] Ibn 'Abd Yalil. Ibn Abi Najih related it from Mujahid.

The fifth: Kinanah ibn 'Abd [ibn] 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Ta'ifi. This was said by al-Suddi.

(p-312) Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said in rebuttal and denunciation of them: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ meaning prophethood, so that they place it wherever they wish, since they have objected to Allah by what they said.

﴿We have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾ The meaning is: since provision is by the decree of Allah, not by the power of a schemer, and this is less than prophethood, how then could prophethood be [distributed by them]? Qatadah said: You find one weak in means, with a stammering tongue, to whom provision has been expanded, and you find one strong in means, eloquent of tongue, upon whom provision is restricted.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have raised some of them above others in degrees﴾ There are two opinions on this: one, by wealth and poverty; the other, by freedom and slavery. ﴿So that some of them may take others in service.﴾ Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Ibn Muhaysin read "sikhriyyan" with a kasra on the sin. Then there are two opinions on this:

One: the rich employ the poor with their wealth, and thus the order of the world is maintained. This is according to the first opinion.

The second: that He makes some of them possessors of others through wealth, so that they take them as slaves. This is according to the second opinion.

(p-313) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾ There are two opinions concerning it. One: prophethood is better than the wealth they amass, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: Paradise is better than what they gather in this world, said by al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾ There are two opinions. One: were it not that they would unite in disbelief, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: upon preferring this world over the religion, said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, roofs of silver﴾ because of the worthlessness of this world in Our sight. Al-Farra' said: If you wish, you may make the lam in "li-buyutihim" repeated, as in His saying: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]; and if you wish, you may make it mean "upon," as if He said: "We would have made for them upon their houses," just as you say to a man: "I made for you, for your people, the gifts," meaning: I made them for them on your account.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "saqfan" in the singular. The rest read "suqufan" with a damma on the sin and the qaf both.

(p-316) The statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whoever turns away﴾. Regarding *yaʿshu* (وَمَن يَعْشُ) there are three opinions.

The first: it means *yuʿrid* (turns away from). This was said by al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Qatadah, al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj also said it.

The second: it means *yaʿma* (becomes blind). This was also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿAta' and Ibn Zayd said it.

The third: that it is weak sight. Al-Mawardi related this. Abu ʿUbaydah said: his eye becomes dim with regard to it. Al-Farra' said: whoever reads *yaʿshu* (with a damma on the shin), its meaning is *yuʿrid*, and whoever reads it with a fatha on the shin (*yaʿshā*), he intends *yaʿma ʿanhu* (becomes blind to it). Ibn Qutaybah said: I do not see the view except the view of Abu ʿUbaydah, and we have not seen anyone permit "ʿashautu ʿan al-shayʾ" (meaning) "aʿrattu ʿanhu" (I turned away from it). What is said is "taʿashaytu ʿan kadhā," meaning "I feigned unawareness of it," as if I had not seen it, and similar to it is "taʿamaytu" (I feigned blindness). The Arabs say "ʿashautu ilā al-nār" when one seeks guidance toward the fire with weak sight. Al-Huṭay'ah said:

*Whenever you come to him, squinting toward the light of his fire,*
*you will find the best fire there, and the best kindler.*

From this is the hadith of Ibn al-Musayyib: "that one of his two eyes had gone, and he was squinting with the other," meaning he sees with it weakly.

The exegetes said: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾, so he does not fear His punishment and does not heed His speech, ﴿We appoint for him﴾, that is, We cause for him, ﴿a devil, and he becomes his companion﴾, who does not leave him; We make that his recompense.

(p-316) ﴿And indeed they﴾, meaning the devils, ﴿bar them﴾, meaning the disbelievers, that is, they prevent them from the path of guidance. He said "they" in the plural because "man" (*man*) is in the place of a plural. ﴿And they think﴾, meaning the disbelieving children of Adam, ﴿that they﴾ are upon guidance.

﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾. Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from ʿAsim read (the variant reading) "jaʾanā" in the singular, meaning the disbeliever. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read "jaʾānā" with two alifs in the dual, meaning the disbeliever and his devil. It has come in the exegesis that on the Day of Resurrection the two will be placed in one chain, and they will not be separated until Allah sends them both to the Fire. ﴿He says﴾, the disbeliever to the devil: ﴿Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts﴾, that is, the distance between the two easts. Regarding these two there are two views.

One: they are the rising point of the sun on the shortest day of the year and its rising point on the longest day. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

The second: he intended the east and the west, and he gave precedence to mention of the east, as they said "sunnat al-ʿUmarayn," meaning Abu Bakr and ʿUmar. They also recited in this respect:

*We took the horizons of the sky over you,*
*for us are its two moons and the rising stars.*

He means the sun and the moon. And they recited:

*The Basra of the Azd is ours, and Iraq is ours,*
*and the two Mosuls, and Egypt and the Hijaz are ours.*

He means the Jazirah and Mosul. [This is the choice of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.]

(p-317) The statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then wretched is the companion﴾, that is, you, O devil. And Allah the Mighty and Majestic says to the disbelievers on that day: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong﴾, that is, you associated partners in the world, ﴿that you will be sharers in the punishment﴾, that is, sharing in the punishment will not benefit you, because each one of them has the greatest share of it. Al-Mubarrad said: they were deprived of the comfort of mutual consolation, because mutual consolation eases the calamity. He recited, for this meaning, the words of al-Khansa', sister of Sakhr ibn Malik:

*Were it not for the multitude of those weeping around me*
*over their brothers, I would have killed myself.*

*They do not weep like my brother,*
*but I console myself for him through consolation.*

Ibn ʿAmir read "innakum" with a kasra on the alif.

Then He informed about them what had preceded for them of wretchedness, with His saying: ﴿Then, are you going to make the deaf hear?﴾ The verse.

**The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 43, verses 41–44:**

The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Then whether We take you away﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: its meaning is "If We take you away." Al-Zajjaj said: the particle "ma" entered as an emphasis on the conditional, and the heavy nun entered "nadhhabanna" also as an emphasis. The meaning is: "We will take revenge upon them if you die, or We will show you what We have promised them and promised you of victory over them." Ibn 'Abbas said: this refers to the Day of Badr. Some exegetes (mufassirun, the scholars of tafsir, meaning Qur'anic interpretation) held that His words ﴿Then whether We take you away﴾ were abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) by the verse of the sword, but there is no basis for this [view].

(p-318) The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And indeed it﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿is a reminder for you﴾, meaning an honour for you by what Allah has granted you, ﴿and for your people﴾. Regarding "your people," there are three opinions. The first: all the Arabs. The second: the Quraysh. The third: all who believed in him. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Prophet ﷺ, when he was asked, 'To whom does this affair belong after you?', would not tell anything until this verse was revealed; after that, whenever he was asked, he would say: 'To the Quraysh.'" This indicates that the Prophet ﷺ understood from this that he would govern the Muslims by virtue of prophethood and the honour of the Qur'an, and that his people would succeed him in authority because of the honour of the Qur'an, which was revealed to a man from among them. The view of Mujahid is that "the people" here are the Arabs, and the Qur'an is an honour for them in that it was revealed in their language. Ibn Qutayba said: "reminder" was used in place of "honour," because the noble is remembered. Regarding His words ﴿and you will be questioned﴾, there are two opinions: the first, about thanking Allah for what you have been given of this; the second, about what obligations (huquq) have become binding upon you concerning it.

**The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 43, verses 45–56:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you﴾. If it is said: how can he ask the messengers when they died before him? There are three answers concerning this.

The first: when he was taken on the Night Journey (isra'), the prophets were gathered for him, and he led them in prayer. Then Jibril (Gabriel) said to him: "Ask those whom We sent before you..." (the verse). He said: "I will not ask; I am content." This was narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas, and it is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri and Ibn Zayd. They said: the messengers were gathered for him on the night he was taken on the Night Journey, he met them, and he was commanded to ask them, but he did not doubt and did not ask.

The second: the intended meaning is: ask the believers among the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) [from] those to whom the prophets were sent. Most exegetes hold that this verse was revealed concerning the dispute of Ibn al-Zib'ara with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when the revelation came: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah...﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. We have explained the story in the commentary on Surah al-Anbiya [21:101]. The polytheists are those who presented ʿIsa as an example for their gods (p-324), and likened him to them, because that verse only included mention of the idols, since they were worshipped besides Allah. So they objected with ʿIsa, presenting him as an example for their idols, because he was an object of worship for the Christians. By "his people" is meant the polytheists.

As for ﴿yasuddun﴾ (يَصِدُّونَ), Ibn ʿAmir, Nafiʿ and al-Kisai read it with a dammah on the ṣād (يَصُدُّونَ), while the rest read it with a kasrah. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of both is the same: they clamour (يَضِجُّونَ). It is possible that the meaning of the form with a dammah is: they turn away (يُعْرِضُونَ). Abu ʿUbayda said: whoever reads it with a kasrah, its majaz (figurative sense) is "they clamour", and whoever reads it with a dammah, its majaz is "they deviate" (يَعْدِلُونَ).

Allah's words: ﴿And they said: Are our gods better, or is he?﴾ The meaning is: they are not better than him. If he is in the Fire because he was worshipped besides Allah, then we are content for our gods to have the same status as him.

﴿They did not present him to you except for disputation﴾, that is: they only mentioned ʿIsa in order to argue with you through him, because they knew that what is meant by "the fuel of Hell" (حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ) is what they took as deities from the dead. ﴿Rather, they are a people given to contention﴾, that is: people of quarrels.

Allah's words: ﴿And We made him an example﴾, that is: a sign and a lesson ﴿for the Children of Israel﴾, by which they would recognise Allah's power over what He wills, since He created him without a father.

(p-325) Then He addressed the disbelievers of Makkah, saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have made from among you﴾. There are two views concerning this.

One of them: the meaning is: We would have made in your place ﴿angels﴾. Then, regarding the meaning of "yakhlifun" (يَخْلُفُونَ, "would succeed/replace"), there are three opinions. The first: some of them would succeed others; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: they would succeed you, to be a replacement in your place; this was said by Mujahid. The third: they would succeed the messengers, so they would be messengers to you in their place; this was related by al-Mawardi.

The second view: the meaning is: "And if We willed, We would have made angels from among you", that is: We would have changed the creation, making some of you angels who would succeed those of you who had gone; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Allah's words: ﴿And indeed he is a sign of the Hour﴾. There are two views concerning the pronoun of the "hā" (the suffix of reference).

One of them: it refers to ʿIsa, peace be upon him. Then, regarding the meaning of the statement, there are two views. The first: the descent of ʿIsa is one of the portents of the Hour, by which its nearness is known; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. The second: the raising of the dead by ʿIsa is evidence of the Hour and the resurrection of the dead; this was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The second view: it refers to the Qur'an; this was said by al-Hasan and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The majority read "la-ʿilm" (لِعِلْمٌ) with a kasrah on the ʿayn and a sukun on the lam. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Razin, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, Qatada, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a fatha on both.

Ibn Qutayba said: whoever reads with a kasrah on the ʿayn, the meaning is that by it the nearness of the Hour is known; and whoever reads with a fatha on the ʿayn and the lam, it means a sign and an indication.

(p-326) Allah's words: ﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾, that is: do not doubt it. ﴿And follow Me﴾ in monotheism. ﴿This﴾, which I am upon, ﴿is a straight path﴾.

﴿And when ʿIsa came with clear proofs﴾. We have explained this in the commentary on Surah al-Baqarah [2:87].

﴿He said: I have come to you with wisdom﴾. On this there are two views. One: prophethood; this was said by ʿAta' and al-Suddi. The second: the Gospel; this was said by Muqatil.

﴿And to make clear to you some of that about which you differ﴾, [that is]: of the matters of your religion. Mujahid said: "some of that about which you differ" refers to the alteration of the Torah. Ibn Jarir said: concerning the rulings of the Torah. Some people have held that "some" (بَعْضَ) here means "all" (الكُلِّ). We have explained this in the commentary on Surah Ghafir [40:28]. Al-Zajjaj said: the correct view is that "some" cannot mean "all", rather ʿIsa made clear to them some of what they differed about, of what they needed. Ibn Jarir also said: there was disagreement among them concerning the matters of their religion and their worldly affairs, so he made clear to them only the matters of their religion. What follows has already been explained [in al-Nisa: 175, Maryam: 37], up to His words: ﴿Do they await...﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah.

﴿They did not present him to you except for disputation﴾, that is: they only mentioned ʿIsa in order to argue with you through him, because they knew that what is meant by "the fuel of Hell" (حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ) is what they took as deities from the dead. ﴿Rather, they are a people given to contention﴾, that is: people of quarrels.

Allah's words: ﴿And We made him an example﴾, that is: a sign and a lesson ﴿for the Children of Israel﴾, by which they would recognise Allah's power over what He wills, since He created him without a father.

(p-325) Then He addressed the disbelievers of Makkah, saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have made from among you﴾. There are two views concerning this.

One of them: the meaning is: We would have made in your place ﴿angels﴾. Then, regarding the meaning of "yakhlifun" (يَخْلُفُونَ, "would succeed/replace"), there are three opinions. The first: some of them would succeed others; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: they would succeed you, to be a replacement in your place; this was said by Mujahid. The third: they would succeed the messengers, so they would be messengers to you in their place; this was related by al-Mawardi.

The second view: the meaning is: "And if We willed, We would have made angels from among you", that is: We would have changed the creation, making some of you angels who would succeed those of you who had gone; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Allah's words: ﴿And indeed he is a sign of the Hour﴾. There are two views concerning the pronoun of the "hā" (the suffix of reference).

One of them: it refers to ʿIsa, peace be upon him. Then, regarding the meaning of the statement, there are two views. The first: the descent of ʿIsa is one of the portents of the Hour, by which its nearness is known; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. The second: the raising of the dead by ʿIsa is evidence of the Hour and the resurrection of the dead; this was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The second view: it refers to the Qur'an; this was said by al-Hasan and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The majority read "la-ʿilm" (لِعِلْمٌ) with a kasrah on the ʿayn and a sukun on the lam. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Razin, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, Qatada, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a fatha on both.

Ibn Qutayba said: whoever reads with a kasrah on the ʿayn, the meaning is that by it the nearness of the Hour is known; and whoever reads with a fatha on the ʿayn and the lam, it means a sign and an indication.

(p-326) Allah's words: ﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾, that is: do not doubt it. ﴿And follow Me﴾ in monotheism. ﴿This﴾, which I am upon, ﴿is a straight path﴾.

﴿And when ʿIsa came with clear proofs﴾. We have explained this in the commentary on Surah al-Baqarah [2:87].

﴿He said: I have come to you with wisdom﴾. On this there are two views. One: prophethood; this was said by ʿAta' and al-Suddi. The second: the Gospel; this was said by Muqatil.

﴿And to make clear to you some of that about which you differ﴾, [that is]: of the matters of your religion. Mujahid said: "some of that about which you differ" refers to the alteration of the Torah. Ibn Jarir said: concerning the rulings of the Torah. Some people have held that "some" (بَعْضَ) here means "all" (الكُلِّ). We have explained this in the commentary on Surah Ghafir [40:28]. Al-Zajjaj said: the correct view is that "some" cannot mean "all", rather ʿIsa made clear to them some of what they differed about, of what they needed. Ibn Jarir also said: there was disagreement among them concerning the matters of their religion and their worldly affairs, so he made clear to them only the matters of their religion. What follows has already been explained [in al-Nisa: 175, Maryam: 37], up to His words: ﴿Do they await...﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah.

[p. 327] His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The close friends﴾, meaning in the worldly life, ﴿on that Day﴾, meaning on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾. This is because friendship that was founded on disbelief and disobedience turns into enmity on the Day of Resurrection. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Umayyah ibn Khalaf and Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. ﴿Except the righteous﴾ means the Muwahhidun (those who affirm the oneness of God). When fear falls upon them on the Day of Resurrection, a caller will call out: ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you today, nor shall you grieve﴾. The creatures will then raise their heads, and he will say: ﴿Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims﴾, and the disbelievers will lower their heads.

[p. 328] Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "Ya 'ibadi" with the yā' affirmed in both states, and with it silent. Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, al-Mufaddal from 'Asim, and Khalaf omitted it in both states.

Regarding ﴿in their spouses﴾ there are two opinions: the first, that they are their wives; the second, that they are their companions.

The meaning of ﴿you will be made joyful﴾ has already been explained [al-Rum: 15].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There will be passed around to them trays of gold﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its singular is ṣaḥfah, which is a large bowl. ﴿And cups﴾: its singular is kūb, which is a round vessel with no handle. Al-Farra' said: the kūb is a [jug] with a round top and no ear (handle). 'Adi said:

Reclining, its doors clapping, a servant moves about him with the kūb.

Ibn Qutayba said: al-akwāb are the ewers that have no handles. Our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: they were without handles so that the drinker could drink from wherever he wished, since a handle would turn the drinker away from some directions.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And therein is what the souls desire﴾ (30). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "tashtahīhi" with an added hā'. Omitting the hā' is, in meaning, the same as affirming it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the eyes delight﴾. It is said: I delighted in the thing (lazztu al-shay'), and I found it delightful (istalazztuhu). The meaning is: there is nothing that a soul desires or that an eye finds delightful that is not in Paradise. God, may He be exalted, has gathered all the bliss of Paradise in these two descriptions, for there is no blessing except that it is a portion of the soul or of the eye. The completion of bliss is eternity, for if it were to end, it would not be pleasant.

[p. 329] ﴿And that is the Paradise﴾, meaning the one He mentioned in His saying: "Enter Paradise", ﴿which you have been given as inheritance﴾. We have explained this in [al-A'raf: 43] at His saying: ﴿you have been given it as inheritance﴾.

Surah 43, verses 74–83

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾, meaning the disbelievers, ﴿will abide in the punishment of Hell﴾ — that is, ﴿it will not be lightened for them, and they therein are despairing﴾, meaning in the punishment, ﴿despairing﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: despairing of the mercy of Allah. We have explained this in [al-An'am: 44]. ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, meaning We did not punish them without a sin, ﴿but they were the wrongdoers﴾ against themselves, by what they committed against their own souls. Al-Zajjaj said: the Basrans say that "hum" here is a fasl (a separating pronoun), and that is what they call it, while the Kufans call it the 'imad (the support pronoun).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik"﴾. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn Ya'mar read "Ya Mali" without the kaf, with the lam kasra. Al-Zajjaj said: the grammarians call this al-tarkhim (apocope, clipping the end of a vocative), but I dislike it because it contradicts the Mushaf.

The exegetes said: they will call upon Malik, the keeper of the Fire, and say: ﴿Let your Lord decree upon us﴾ (p-330) [that is]: let Him cause us to die. The meaning is that they sought his intercession so that he would ask Allah for death for them, that they might find rest from the punishment. He then remains silent in answer to them for a period, and concerning the length of that period there are four opinions. The first: forty years, said by Abdullah ibn Amr and Muqatil. The second: thirty years, said by Anas. The third: a thousand years, said by Ibn Abbas. The fourth: one hundred years, said by Ka'b.

The meaning is that they sought his intercession so that he would ask Allah for death for them, that they might find rest from the punishment. He then remains silent in answer to them for a period, and concerning the length of that period there are four opinions. The first: forty years, said by Abdullah ibn Amr and Muqatil. The second: thirty years, said by Anas. The third: a thousand years, said by Ibn Abbas. The fourth: one hundred years, said by Ka'b.

Concerning his silence in answer to them for this period there are two views. The first: he remained silent until Allah revealed to him to answer them, said by Muqatil. The second: because the distance between the call and the answer is more humiliating and degrading for them.

Al-Mawardi said: Malik then answered them, saying: ﴿Indeed, you will remain﴾, that is, you will abide in the punishment.

﴿Indeed, We have brought you the truth﴾, that is, We sent Our messengers with monotheism, ﴿but most of you are averse to the truth﴾. Ibn Abbas said: he means all of you, ﴿averse﴾ to what Muhammad ﷺ brought.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or have they determined a matter?﴾ Regarding "am" there are two views. The first: it is interrogative. The second: it means "bal" (rather). Al-ibram means firm determination. Concerning this matter there are three opinions.

The first: the plot against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to kill him or expel him, when they gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (the council house); the account has already been explained [al-Anfal: 30]. This was said by most of the scholars.

The second: that it is the firm resolve of their affair in denying (the truth), said by Qatadah.

The third: that it is the firm resolve of their affair that will save them from the punishment, said by al-Farra'.

(p-331) ﴿Then indeed, We are the determiners﴾, that is, We firmly decree a matter concerning their recompense.

﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret﴾, which is what they keep hidden from others, ﴿and their private conversation﴾, what they confide to one another, ﴿Yes, [We do hear]﴾. The meaning is: We do hear that, ﴿and Our messengers with them are writing﴾, meaning [from] the guardian angels.

﴿Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers"﴾. Regarding "in" there are two views.

The first: it is conditional, and the meaning is: if He had a son in your claim and by your assumption. On this reading, concerning His saying ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ there are four opinions.

The first: "then I would be the first of the deniers," narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. In another narration from Ibn Abbas: two Bedouins brought a dispute before him, and one of them said: "This man had land in his possession which he worked for me." Ibn Abbas said: "Allahu Akbar! Then I am the first of the worshippers who deny that Allah has a son."

The second: "then I would be the first to worship Allah in opposition to your saying," said by Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: if you claim that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first of the monotheists.

The third: "then I would be the first of those who are disdainful toward Allah regarding what you say," said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Abu Ubaydah. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said "I disdained from such-and-such" (ʿabidtu min kadha, a'bidu, 'abadan), so I am ʿabad and ʿabid. Al-Farazdaq said:

(p-332)
"Those are a people, if they satirize me, I satirize them, / and I am too disdainful that Tamim be satirized by Darim"

meaning: I am too proud (ānaf). Abu Ubaydah recited:

"And I am too disdainful to revile them in front of my people, / and I prefer Darim and the Banu Rizah."

The fourth: the meaning of the verse is: just as I am not the first worshipper of Allah, so He has no son. This is like saying: "If you are a scribe, then I am a reckoner," meaning: you are not a scribe and neither am I a reckoner. Al-Wahidi related this view from Sufyan ibn Uyaynah.

The second view: "in" means "ma" (not), said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. The meaning would then be: the Most Merciful had no son, so I am the first to worship Allah with certainty that He has no son. Abu Ubaydah said: on this view the fa' (then) is in the sense of waw (and).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So leave them﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿to plunge in vanity and to play﴾ in their worldly life, ﴿until they meet﴾ their Day. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza, Ibn Muhaysin, and Abu Ja'far read "hatta yalqaw" with a fatha on the ya and qaf, a sukun on the lam, without an alif. The intended meaning is: they meet [the Day of] Resurrection. This verse, according to the majority, is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 43, verse 84–89:

Allah's saying: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: He is worshipped in the heaven and worshipped on the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: He is the One God in the heaven and on the earth. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Sumaifaʿ, Ibn Yaʿmar, and al-Jahdari recited: "fi al-samaʾi Allahu wa fi al-ardi Allahu," with the alif and lam, without tanwin and without hamza in either of them. What follows of this has already been explained [in al-Aʿraf: 54, Luqman: 34], up to His saying: ﴿Those whom they invoke besides Him have no power of intercession﴾. The occasion of its revelation was that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and a group with him said: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we will take the angels as allies, for they are more deserving of intercession than Muhammad." So this verse was revealed. This is related by Muqatil.

There are two views regarding the meaning of the verse.

The first: He intended by "those they invoke besides Him" their gods, then He made an exception of Jesus, Ezra, and the angels, saying: ﴿except one who testifies to the truth﴾, which is to bear witness that there is no god but Allah, ﴿and they know﴾ with their hearts what they testify to with their tongues. This is the view of the majority, among them Qatadah.

The second: The intended meaning of "those who invoke" is Jesus, Ezra, and the angels whom the polytheists worshipped besides Allah; these do not possess intercession for anyone, ﴿except one who testifies﴾, i.e., [except] for one who testifies ﴿to the truth﴾, which is the word of sincerity, ﴿and they know﴾ that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created Jesus, Ezra, and the angels. This is the view of a group, among them Mujahid. In the verse there is evidence that the condition for all testimonies is that the witness must have knowledge of what he testifies to.

Allah's saying: ﴿And [He has knowledge of] his saying, "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe"﴾. Qatadah said: This is your Prophet complaining of his people to his Lord. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He complained to Allah of his people's refusal to believe. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, and Abu ʿAmr recited: "wa qilahu" with a fatha on the lam; and in it there are three aspects.

The first: He implied a verb with it, as if He said: "And he said his saying," and he complained his complaint to his Lord.

The second: It is conjoined to His saying: "Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk and their saying?" So the meaning is: and We hear his saying. Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash mentioned both views.

The third: It is in the accusative on the sense of: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour" and He knows his saying, because the meaning of "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour" is: He knows the Hour and He knows his saying. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj. ʿAsim and Hamzah recited: "wa qilihi," with a kasra on the lam and the ha' until it reaches the ya'; and the meaning is: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of his saying." Abu Hurayrah, Abu Razin, (p-335) Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Abu Raja', al-Jahdari, Qatadah, and Humayd recited with a damma on the lam; and the meaning is: his calling is this word: "My Lord." Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj mentioned the reason for the kasra and the damma.

Allah's saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, i.e., turn away from them, ﴿and say, "Peace"﴾. In it there are three views.

The first: Say good in place of their evil. This is said by al-Suddi.

The second: Return to them kindness. This is said by Muqatil.

The third: Say that by which you will be safe from their evil. This is related by al-Mawardi.

﴿But they will come to know﴾. In it there are three views. The first: they will come to know the consequence of their disbelief. The second: that you are truthful. The third: the descent of punishment upon them, and this is a threat to them: "But they will come to know." Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir recited "taʿlamun" with the ta'. Whoever recites with the ya', it is a command to the Prophet ﷺ to address them with this, as said by Muqatil; then the verse of the sword abrogated the turning away and the peace.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 43, verse 84–89:

Allah's saying: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: He is worshipped in the heaven and worshipped on the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: He is the One God in the heaven and on the earth. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Sumaifaʿ, Ibn Yaʿmar, and al-Jahdari recited: "fi al-samaʾi Allahu wa fi al-ardi Allahu," with the alif and lam, without tanwin and without hamza in either of them. What follows of this has already been explained [in al-Aʿraf: 54, Luqman: 34], up to His saying: ﴿Those whom they invoke besides Him have no power of intercession﴾. The occasion of its revelation was that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and a group with him said: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we will take the angels as allies, for they are more deserving of intercession than Muhammad." So this verse was revealed. This is related by Muqatil.

There are two views regarding the meaning of the verse.

The first: He intended by "those they invoke besides Him" their gods, then He made an exception of Jesus, Ezra, and the angels, saying: ﴿except one who testifies to the truth﴾, which is to bear witness that there is no god but Allah, ﴿and they know﴾ with their hearts what they testify to with their tongues. This is the view of the majority, among them Qatadah.

The second: The intended meaning of "those who invoke" is Jesus, Ezra, and the angels whom the polytheists worshipped besides Allah; these do not possess intercession for anyone, ﴿except one who testifies﴾, i.e., [except] for one who testifies ﴿to the truth﴾, which is the word of sincerity, ﴿and they know﴾ that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created Jesus, Ezra, and the angels. This is the view of a group, among them Mujahid. In the verse there is evidence that the condition for all testimonies is that the witness must have knowledge of what he testifies to.

Allah's saying: ﴿And [He has knowledge of] his saying, "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe"﴾. Qatadah said: This is your Prophet complaining of his people to his Lord. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He complained to Allah of his people's refusal to believe. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, and Abu ʿAmr recited: "wa qilahu" with a fatha on the lam; and in it there are three aspects.

The first: He implied a verb with it, as if He said: "And he said his saying," and he complained his complaint to his Lord.

The second: It is conjoined to His saying: "Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk and their saying?" So the meaning is: and We hear his saying. Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash mentioned both views.

The third: It is in the accusative on the sense of: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour" and He knows his saying, because the meaning of "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour" is: He knows the Hour and He knows his saying. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj. ʿAsim and Hamzah recited: "wa qilihi," with a kasra on the lam and the ha' until it reaches the ya'; and the meaning is: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of his saying." Abu Hurayrah, Abu Razin, (p-335) Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Abu Raja', al-Jahdari, Qatadah, and Humayd recited with a damma on the lam; and the meaning is: his calling is this word: "My Lord." Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj mentioned the reason for the kasra and the damma.

Allah's saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, i.e., turn away from them, ﴿and say, "Peace"﴾. In it there are three views.

The first: Say good in place of their evil. This is said by al-Suddi.

The second: Return to them kindness. This is said by Muqatil.

The third: Say that by which you will be safe from their evil. This is related by al-Mawardi.

﴿But they will come to know﴾. In it there are three views. The first: they will come to know the consequence of their disbelief. The second: that you are truthful. The third: the descent of punishment upon them, and this is a threat to them: "But they will come to know." Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir recited "taʿlamun" with the ta'. Whoever recites with the ya', it is a command to the Prophet ﷺ to address them with this, as said by Muqatil; then the verse of the sword abrogated the turning away and the peace.
